gaps.sentence: The referee warned the players not to ___ the rules.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'rules' (the referee warns against it)
gaps.explanation: break the rules means to disobey them; the context ('warned not to') requires this meaning.

gaps.sentence: I was nearly late, but I managed to ___ the last bus.
gaps.hint: to get on a bus or train in time
gaps.explanation: catch a bus/train means to arrive in time to board it; the words 'managed to' and 'nearly late' show success.

gaps.sentence: Most children learn to ___ the time before they start school.
gaps.hint: fixed phrase: ___ the time (read a clock)
gaps.explanation: tell the time means to be able to read a clock; it is a fixed expression.

gaps.sentence: Unlike some politicians, she ___ her promises.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'promises' (she is unlike other politicians)
gaps.explanation: keep a promise means to do what you promised; the contrast with other politicians shows the positive verb.

gaps.sentence: A true friend will always ___ a secret.
gaps.explanation: keep a secret is the fixed collocation for not telling it to anyone.

gaps.sentence: Over five hundred athletes will ___ part in the games.
gaps.explanation: take part in something means to participate in it.

gaps.sentence: He was so badly ___ in the fall that he needed an operation.
gaps.explanation: badly hurt is the standard collocation meaning seriously injured.

gaps.sentence: All candidates must ___ the written exam in June.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'exam' from the candidate's side
gaps.explanation: take an exam (or sit an exam) means to be tested; 'give an exam' is not used in British English.
